summary: Redwood demo focused on mapping SwiftBridge's OpenAI/Anthropic/Together endpoints to Redwood API equivalents, discussion of performance and cost tradeoffs, and next steps to kick off a short pilot and security review.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on the account, and Ethan our SE will walk through the parity mapping and runtime choices. Quick sound check?
[00:18] Lena Ortiz (SwiftBridge): Yep, loud and clear. Thanks.
[00:22] Ethan Cole (Redwood SE): Great, I'll share my screen in a second. The agenda: map your current OpenAI/Anthropic/Together endpoints to Redwood API calls, show the console and Optimize suggestions, then talk pilot scope.
[00:38] Marcus Han (SwiftBridge): That sounds good. Our immediate goal is to see parity for our customer-facing chat and reranker microservices, and then an internal embeddings store.
[00:49] Maya: Perfect. Quick context check — you currently run mixed production: chat on OpenAI, some vetting with Anthropic for safety layers, and Together for cheaper throughput on batch jobs. True?
[01:02] Lena: Yup. Chat is on GPT-like endpoints, Anthropic for a few safety flows, Together for nightly embedding jobs because it's cheaper.
[01:12] Tommy Ruiz (SwiftBridge): And we have a 150ms p95 target for the chat path, 99.9 uptime, and a hard cost budget we can't exceed.
[01:23] Ethan: Good callouts. Okay I'll switch to the parity spreadsheet — apologies if the model names are a little fuzzy, I typed quick notes.
[01:30] [screen share noise]
[01:34] Ethan: So on the left you can see your OpenAI calls: completions and chat. Middle column is the Anthropic safety wrapper, and right is Together for bulk embed. Column four is our recommended Redwood API mapping; basically same calls, a small adapter layer. For instance your OpenAI chat -> Redwood chat endpoint, same input format mostly, we do support function calling and streaming.
[01:55] Lena: Do you preserve the roles and message deltas? We rely on delta encoding to keep tokens down.
[02:03] Ethan: Yes, Redwood maintains role messages and incremental streaming; the delta semantics are preserved. We also have a prefix/K-V cache that can cache the system prompt and shared context which usually reduces token egress by 20-40% depending on stickiness.
[02:18] Marcus: K-V cash?
[02:20] Ethan: K-V cache, sorry — sometimes STT jokes — keee-v cash.
[02:25] [small laugh]
[02:27] Priya Singh (SwiftBridge): From security perspective, we need to understand data residency and key management. Do you support customer-managed keys in hosted?
[02:36] Maya: Short answer yes for Private and Dedicated we integrate with KMS/HSM; for Hosted API we offer envelope encryption and bring-your-own-key patterns via partner KMS in certain regions — we'll send exact pr docs.
[02:49] Priya: And audit logs, long-term retention?
[02:52] Ethan: Console exposes audit trails per model and per route; we can stream logs to your SIEM, and retention is configurable as an add-on. We'll include the retention grid in the security packet.
[03:05] Lena: Cool. On the model side, Anthropic has a different safety footprint; do you recommend a model variant for safety-critical flows?
[03:14] Ethan: We do have Redwood-curated safer variants and you can chain a safety model in a canary route. Also Redwood Optimize will flag output-quality regressions if switching model versions. For Anthropic-like behavior we recommend the "safety-tuned" family in our catalog — names in the parity sheet.
[03:30] Marcus: What about latency — Together for bulk is cheaper but sometimes has slower tail latency. Can Redwood route requests by policy?
[03:39] Maya: Yes, smart routing is supported. You can route by latency SLO, cost, or region. For example, low-latency chat goes to Dedicated hosts in us-west with hot-cache; bulk embeddings can go to cheaper on-demand pools with longer tails.
[03:55] Ethan: Also worth noting our continuous batching works differently; for synchronous chat we maintain micro-batching to hit latency SLOs while reducing unit cost. For your traffic shape, we'll recommend batching thresholds in the Optimize tab.
[04:10] Marcus: Can you simulate our traffic shape?
[04:13] Ethan: We can. That's part of the pilot — we run your representative replay on Redwood test cluster and show p95, tokens/sec, and cost. We'll need a 48-hour sample or synthetic profile.
[04:24] Tommy: We'll provide 72 hours of anonymized traces.
[04:28] Ethan: Perfect.
[04:30] [45 sec pause while Ethan navigates console]
[04:58] Ethan: On the console, this is the route config screen — you can pin a model version, set a fallback policy (e.g., fallback to a cheaper quantized variant), and specify batch sizing and TTL for prefix cache.
[05:12] Lena: Fallbacks — do they preserve deterministic behavior? We've had flakiness when falling back to smaller quantized models.
[05:20] Ethan: Good call. Fallbacks are for availability — we recommend canarying and also an automatic quality gate. If the fallback diverges beyond threshold, traffic is diverted to the last good model. That's configurable per route.
[05:33] Priya: Do you have SSO and RBAC interfaces? We need scoping for auditors.
[05:39] Maya: Yes: SAML/SSO, fine-grained RBAC, and token-level permissions. We'll include screenshots of role templates in the packet.
[05:48] Marcus: On cost math: how do you show token-level breakdown? Our current invoices are hard to parse across vendors.
[05:56] Ethan: Console has per-request token breakdown and cost estimator. In the parity sheet we included a sample of your current bills (we redacted) and mapped to Redwood's expected token pricing and quantized variant costs. Usually you see 10-30% unit cost improvement after caching + batching + quantization.
[06:16] Lena: That sounds promising but we'll want a tight guardrail on latency.
[06:20] Maya: Totally — pilot will be latency-focused for chat and throughput-focused for embeddings. We usually do a 3-day run: day 1 smoke, day 2 ramp, day 3 steady-state.
[06:30] Tommy: About private deployment — we have internal regs that might require VPC-only access in EU2. How heavy is the on-prem package?
[06:38] Ethan: For VPC we deploy a private control plane with customer-managed network. The on-prem stack is heavier — usually for air-gapped customers — and includes an ops runbook. For your case if it's VPC in region EU2, it's a lighter integration. We'll draft a network diagram.
[06:52] [background: someone typing]
[06:55] Marcus: A practical question: how much code change? Our platform currently wraps OpenAI/Anthropic SDKs.
[07:02] Ethan: Minimal. We provide a drop-in adapter library and examples to translate telemetry and retries. Most teams change the webhook and a small auth shim. We have an adapter repo on GitHub — link in the notes.
[07:15] Lena: Will function calling maps be 1:1? We heavily use structured function outputs.
[07:21] Ethan: Yes, function call semantics are supported. A few edge cases: ambiguous field names sometimes require a small mapping layer, but nothing major. We'll show a sample mapping during the pilot.
[07:33] Priya: Any concerns with PII or retention during pilot?
[07:36] Maya: We'll sign a pilot NDA and you can opt to scrub PII or run entirely on Private if needed. For Hosted pilot, we can enable stricter retention and KMS controls.
[07:48] Lena: Great. Can you walk through an example of the Optimize suggestions?
[07:52] Ethan: Sure — switching to the Optimize tab. The analyzer detected repeated system prompts and suggested pinning them into prefix cache with a TTL of 24 hours. It also suggested quantized 4bit variant for nightly embedding jobs and a smaller context window for summarization tasks. Attached is the explain plan.
[08:14] Marcus: Quantization — do you preserve embedding quality? Our similarity recall needs to be stable.
[08:19] Ethan: We run evals against your gold set; most embedding quantization leaves similarity >98% for the models we recommend. We'll include evaluation reports.
[08:29] [crosstalk: Lena and Tommy]
[08:34] Maya: Ok wrapping into next steps: we'll send the detailed parity spreadsheet, SOC2 + ISO pack, sample adapter code, and a proposed pilot schedule. Can we confirm target decision timeline?
[08:46] Lena: We'd like a pilot next week and evaluate in two weeks. Target decision by end of May.
[08:52] Maya: Sounds good. Any blockers?
[08:55] Priya: I'll need the compliance artifact list.
[08:57] Maya: On it — action item.
[08:59] Marcus: I'll upload traffic traces and p95 targets by Friday.
[09:03] Maya: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the pilot kickoff and the private deployment deep-dive.
[09:11] Ethan: One last note — I'll attach a short script showing the few-line adapter to swap OpenAI calls to Redwood for your engineers.
[09:20] Lena: Thanks all.
[09:22] [meeting ends]

Notes: transcript has occasional misspellings and speaker attribution may be imperfect. Links mentioned: parity sheet (internal): https://redwood.app/parity/swiftbridge-83421, adapter repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/adapter-examples, security packet placeholder: https://redwood.app/secpack/83421
